claims.feature: other: no one-to-one mapping onto real people
claims.claim: Kay says he never wants to write a book where things map directly, with a character mapping onto a real person or an event onto a real event.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Margins of History', Locus interview excerpt
claims.quote: I don’t ever want to write a book where things map directly

claims.claim: Kay says of The Last Light of the Sun's northern setting that silk does not work in the northlands, and that mosaics, silk, delicate jewellery and philosophy do not fit that world.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'View from the North', Locus interview excerpts (full interview April 2004 issue)
claims.quote: Silk doesn't work in the northlands

claims.feature: other: competing versions of one story
claims.claim: Kay says the vast gulf between how the Uskoks were seen by Venice and Dubrovnik and how they understood themselves is very fertile ground for a novelist.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Chris Urie, Clarkesworld issue 117
claims.quote: That kind of gap is very fertile ground for a novelist

claims.feature: other: under-explored corners of the record
claims.claim: Kay says he likes finding corners of history that have been under-explored.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Chris Urie, Clarkesworld issue 117
claims.quote: I like finding corners of history that have been under-explored

claims.claim: Kay says that with calligraphy in River of Stars, as earlier with mosaic, he wanted to reveal expertise and craft by focusing on technical details.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Rob Rhodes, FantasyLiterature
claims.quote: reveal expertise and craft by focusing on technical details

claims.claim: Kay says that often as a nation or empire diminishes its administrative rigidity grows, and that this is true of the bureaucracy in River of Stars.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Rob Rhodes, FantasyLiterature
claims.quote: Often as a nation or empire diminishes, its administrative rigidity grows

claims.claim: Kay says a reader who does not know Fionavar stands to the back-story as his characters stand to the millennial love triangle, so that we almost get it but not quite.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Patrick St-Denis (fantasyhotlist)
claims.quote: We almost get it, but not quite
claims.page: answer on bringing Fionavar characters into Ysabel

claims.claim: Kay names language as a third element alongside character and drama in the pairing that defines a novel he enjoys, and says he writes in that direction.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Patrick St-Denis (fantasyhotlist)
claims.quote: language is a third element

claims.feature: other: not talking down to the reader
claims.claim: Kay says he is drawn to intelligent characters and gets irritated if he feels too much smarter than the characters, unless that is done with purpose.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Patrick St-Denis (fantasyhotlist)
claims.quote: I get irritated if I feel too much smarter than the characters
